analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in federal waters off Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Florida's two Democratic senators, got a Senate committee hearing in July 2001 but never a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from leasing any federal waters in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic up to the Florida-Georgia border for oil, gas, or mineral drilling [S2][S3]. It would also require a full environmental impact statement and a state "consistency certification" before any offshore lease option could be sold, and would let the Interior Department buy back about $90 million worth of existing undeveloped leases near Florida's coast, paying the leaseholders for those rights [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal residents, tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing interests, whose beaches, waters, and economies would be shielded from drilling spills, rigs, and onshore infrastructure. The state also gains a formal veto-like checkpoint, since leases could not proceed without a state consistency certification under the Coastal Zone Management Act [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities, tourism, and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, Straits of Florida, and South Atlantic planning areas off Florida

Requires a National Environmental Policy Act environmental impact statement and a state consistency certification before an option to lease (including exploratory wells) could be sold, giving Florida and the public a formal review role

Authorizes the Interior Secretary to buy back outstanding undeveloped leases in the Destin Dome, Desoto Canyon, Pensacola, and other near-Florida areas for a total of about $90.2 million, removing existing drilling rights close to the coast

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that hold or seek leases in the prohibited areas: they would lose access to those waters for exploration and production, though the bill's buyback provision would compensate holders of the listed existing leases at roughly $90 million in federal funds, i.e., taxpayer money [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; taxpayers fund the buyback

drawbacks.text: The bill forecloses domestic oil and gas production in these federal waters, which industry and energy-security advocates would argue reduces domestic supply and federal royalty revenue
The buyback authorizes up to $90,162,402 in appropriations to pay oil and gas companies for their existing lease rights, a direct cost to federal taxpayers

The added environmental impact statement and state consistency requirements would slow and complicate leasing even outside the banned areas, including the natural-gas carve-out's absence from review (the environmental-review requirements do not apply to plans for natural gas production and transportation)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida's coastal economy, the bill traded a modest, one-time public cost (about $90 million to buy back existing leases) for a permanent drilling ban and stronger environmental review. The main cost falls on oil and gas companies' access to those waters, and the bill quietly exempts natural gas production-and-transportation plans from its toughest review requirements — a concession that slightly weakens the environmental safeguards. On balance, the design favors coastal protection while compensating rather than expropriating existing leaseholders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held a hearing in July 2001 but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and it died when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham, joined by Sen. Bill Nelson, introduced the bill in the Senate on April 25, 2001
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day
The committee held hearings on the bill on July 12, 2001
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired with the 107th Congress in January 2003

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests kept their ability to seek and hold leases in the eastern Gulf and near-Florida waters, and the permanent ban and buyback never became law. Florida's coastal communities got no federal statutory protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas leaseholders and drilling interests

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 771 on April 25, 2001 to permanently ban offshore drilling off Florida and gave introductory remarks

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, which was introduced for Graham and Nelson together

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on July 12, 2001 but never reported it out or scheduled a markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Both Florida sponsors were Democrats and the bill drew only that one cosponsor, but no floor or committee vote was ever recorded, so no partisan split can be measured; the opposing side's actions never appear in the congressional record.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes the eastern Gulf, Straits of Florida, and South Atlantic planning areas to leasing and would have paid existing leaseholders about $90 million to give up near-shore leases. Its interest in opening these waters runs directly against Florida's coastal economy and environment.
Beach-dependent tourism depends on unpolluted coastlines and unobstructed ocean views; a permanent drilling ban protects the beaches and waters the industry sells to visitors.
The bill protects fisheries and marine habitats in the Gulf and South Atlantic planning areas from drilling spills and platform development, and names fisheries among its subjects.
